procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Calcutta High Court dated March 28, 1968, quashing the processes issued against the three accused persons.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
2. The complainant moved the Sessions Judge, Purulia, against the order of dismissal.
3. A reference was made to the Calcutta High Court.
4. A Single Judge of the Calcutta High Court accepted the reference, set aside the order of the Magistrate, and sent the case back for proceeding in accordance with law.
5. The High Court, in a petition to quash the issue of process, held that the Sub-Divisional Magistrate had no right to issue process since he was not the Magistrate who had taken cognizance of the offence and also observed that the evidence in the case came from tainted sources.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision to quash the process against T. Ganguly.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, who has not taken cognizance of an offence and to whom the case has not been transferred, has the jurisdiction to issue process under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: A complaint was filed, and a Magistrate, Shri S. K. Ganguly, took cognizance of the case and conducted a judicial enquiry.
After the enquiry, Shri Ganguly concluded that a prima facie case had been made out and submitted a report to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM), Purulia.
The SDM, upon receiving the report, issued a process (an order to compel the attendance of the accused).
The High Court quashed this process, reasoning that the SDM had no right to issue it because he was not the Magistrate who had originally taken cognizance of the offence.
law: The Supreme Court identified two legal pathways under the Code of Criminal Procedure for a Magistrate to issue a process:
1. Under Section 204, the Magistrate who takes cognizance of an offence can issue a process.
2. Under Section 202, a Magistrate to whom a case has been transferred by the Magistrate who took cognizance can issue a process.

The court emphasized that the issuance of a process is a matter of judicial determination, which is why the power is specifically granted to the Magistrate who has either taken cognizance or has been officially assigned the case through a transfer.
application: The Court applied these legal principles to the facts of the case.
It was established that Magistrate Shri Ganguly was the one who took cognizance of the offence, not the SDM who issued the process.
Therefore, the SDM could not have issued the process under Section 204.
The Court also found that there was no order transferring the case from Shri Ganguly to the SDM.
Consequently, the SDM also lacked the authority to issue the process under Section 202.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since the Magistrate who issued the process had neither taken cognizance of the offence nor had the case been transferred to him, he lacked the jurisdiction to issue the process. The Court, therefore, affirmed the High Court's decision to quash the process.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercising its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can examine the evidence to determine if a prima facie case is established when considering a petition to quash proceedings.

facts: The appellant argued that the High Court, when considering a petition to quash proceedings, should not have examined whether a prima facie case was established.
The High Court had observed that the evidence in the case came from "tainted sources" and was not reliable.
law: The Supreme Court affirmed that under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court has the power to examine whether there is any legal evidence to support the proceedings.
application: The Supreme Court interpreted the High Court's finding that the evidence was from "tainted sources" and unreliable. It reasoned that this was equivalent to a finding of "no case to go to the jury."

This assessment was not an improper weighing of evidence but rather a determination of whether any legal evidence existed to sustain the case, which is a permissible inquiry under the High Court's inherent powers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was correct in exercising its inherent powers under Section 561-A to examine the evidence to determine if there was any legal basis for the case to proceed, thereby accepting that the High Court can undertake such an examination.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, who has not taken cognizance of an offence and to whom the case has not been transferred, has the jurisdiction to issue process under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the power to issue process is not limited to the Magistrate who takes cognizance under Section 204. They contended that a Magistrate to whom a case is transferred can also issue process under Section 202, implying that the Sub-Divisional Magistrate's order to issue process was legally valid.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (Shri S. Sarkar) had no right to issue process under Section 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because he was not the Magistrate who had taken cognizance of the offence (Shri S. K. Ganguly).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercising its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can examine the evidence to determine if a prima facie case is established when considering a petition to quash proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position implies that the High Court should not have delved into the evidence. They would argue that once the enquiring Magistrate found a prima facie case, the High Court should not re-evaluate the evidence at the stage of a quashing petition, as that is a matter for trial.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the High Court was justified in examining the evidence to determine if a prima facie case existed. This is supported by the High Court's observation that the evidence came from 'tainted sources', indicating that the court should exercise its inherent power to quash proceedings that are an abuse of the legal process.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to issue a process is a judicial determination that can only be made by the magistrate who has taken cognizance of the offense or by a magistrate to whom the case has been formally transferred.
obiter: Under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court has the authority to assess whether there is any legal evidence to support a case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was correct to quash the issue of process. The Magistrate who issued the process lacked jurisdiction because he had neither taken cognizance of the offence nor had the case been formally transferred to him. Furthermore, the High Court acted within its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to examine the evidence and was justified in concluding that the evidence, coming from tainted sources, was insufficient to establish a prima facie case.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 204, Cr.P.C., the Magistrate who takes cognizance of an offence is empowered to issue process.
Under Section 202, Cr.P.C., a Magistrate to whom a case has been transferred can issue process.

Under Section 561-A, Cr.P.C., the High Court has the inherent power to go into the question as to whether there is any legal evidence to support a prima facie case, and can quash proceedings if the evidence is found to be wholly unreliable, akin to a finding of 'no case to go to the jury'.
why_appellant_lost: The Magistrate who issued the process had not taken cognizance of the offence, and there was no order transferring the case to him, rendering the issuance of process invalid.

The appellant's contention that the High Court should not have examined the evidence was rejected, as the Supreme Court affirmed that the High Court's power under Section 561-A includes assessing whether any legal evidence exists to sustain the proceedings.
why_respondent_won: The Magistrate who issued the process (Shri Sarkar) was not the Magistrate who took cognizance (Shri Ganguly), and the case was never formally transferred to him, meaning he lacked the jurisdiction to issue the process.

The High Court was justified in exercising its inherent power under Section 561-A to examine the evidence and quash the proceedings, as its finding that the evidence came from 'tainted sources' and was unreliable was a valid determination that no prima facie case was established.
policy_considerations: The issue of process is a matter for judicial determination that requires the Magistrate to have properly engaged with the case, which is why the power is restricted to the Magistrate who has taken cognizance or the one to whom the case has been formally transferred.

The inherent power of the High Court under Section 561-A serves to prevent the abuse of legal process by allowing it to quash proceedings where the evidence is so fundamentally flawed ('tainted sources') that it amounts to no legal evidence at all.
